posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Waming the water softens the gel and allows the gel to expand more.

And think of heating the alcohol as causing that particular concentration to work faster.

Changing the temp of either will affect the final outcome.

> Say for example a hologram is made with a warmer water bath, and a cooler alcohol bath. Then, in another test, this was reversed by making the water cooler, and the alcohol warmer. Would the end result be the same?

No, cooler alcohols gives a narrower band holograms and warmer baths gives broaderband holograms. But this can be slightly offset by the time in the baths. Longer pushes toward narrower band and shorter pushes toward wider band. Now if you put the hologram in warm water first and soften it, and then try to process it with cool long baths you are kind of working against yourself. Same with the reverse. 

I try to keep my water the coolest of all baths including the alcohols and either keep the subsiquent bath the same or warmer depending on what I want.

Example. If my water is 78F the each bath after that is the same or warmer. If I want to use cool, 68F alcohols, then I use my water at 68F also.

Oh, this also includes the fixer temps since it is the first bath. It is always the coolest or same.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Joe Farina:** I did some tests today, and was wondering if there is any reason to heat the subsequent alcohol bath(s), instead of the initial water soak. It seems to me that it essentially does the same thing. I figured that if the alcohol didn't need to be heated, it would be a good thing.

Speculating about the effect of hot (vs. cold) alcohol, it'll dehydrate the gelatin much more quickly.

And in the context of the “void theory”, hot alcohol might

1) significantly heat up the layer (when the water soaked layer encounters 100% alcohol);

2) form larger voids;

3) more diverse (polydisperse) void size which might lead to the large broad bandwidths so typical to DCG. My guess would be that the largest voids will build up on the surface.

Moreover, hot alcohol may be analog to hot (silver halide) developer. So it would be likely to be much more active. The amplification of the latent image will become more enhanced and hence it might require less light exposure to form an image.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: I was told by a former significant at Hughes that they did not heat their alcohol baths because of liability and environmental issues in California. He said that if you don't harden as much in earlier steps, the alcohol baths could be at room temperature. I don't have any other details.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **BobH:** I was told by a former significant at Hughes that they did not heat their alcohol baths because of liability and environmental issues in California. He said that if you don't harden as much in earlier steps, the alcohol baths could be at room temperature. I don't have any other details.

That's interesting. In my simplistic view, heat is heat. But of course gelatin swells in water and not alcohol, so maybe that will account for differences in behavior. I may be completely wrong, but it seemed that warm water tends to result in white broadband holograms, while hot alcohol tends to result in golden broadband holograms (?) The results I got from warm water were so good that I don't see the need for hot alcohol right now, and I seem to recall that breathing hot IPA fumes is best avoided, if possible. My lab has a good exhaust fan, but if I turn it on, my lab temperature will go sharply down, as it's about 20F outside right now.

I've been paying attention to environmental factors as I make DCG holograms, and I think it's essential to keep track of them (temperature and humidity). Since I'm working in a former garage, it's pretty tight in there, and just the act of breathing and body temperature seem to have a noticeable effect (especially if I'm working hard )

He said that if you don't harden as much in earlier steps, the alcohol baths could be at room temperature. I don't have any other details.

There's an Agfa patent on DCG that recommends a mixture of sodium bisulfite + formaldehyde for development. Such treatment was said to produce very low noise holograms. Moreover, the IPA baths were kept at room temperature.

I guess formaldehyde hardening – though not quite the number one agent to use in respect to environmental/health considerations – is interesting, because its crosslinking action may not interfere with chrome hardening.
